grep: Searches for specific patterns or text strings within files and outputs matching lines.
cd: Changes the current working directory in the command-line interface.
wget: A non-interactive network downloader used to retrieve files from the web via HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP.
curl: A command-line tool for transferring data to or from a server using various protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, etc.
ls: Lists directory contents, showing files and folders inside the current working directory.
pwd: Prints the absolute path of the current working directory.
mkdir: Creates a new directory or folder at the specified location.
chmod: Changes file or directory access permissions in Unix-like operating systems.
chown: Changes the user and group ownership of file system files and directories.
iptables: A user-space application program that allows a system administrator to configure the IP packet filter rules of the Linux kernel firewall.
systemctl: A command-line tool to inspect and manage the systemd system and service manager.
linux: A free and open-source Unix-like operating system kernel first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
unix: A family of multitasking, multiuser operating systems originally developed at Bell Labs in the 1970s.
kernel: The core of an operating system that manages hardware, memory, processes, and system calls.
shell: A command-line interpreter that provides an interface for users to interact with the operating system.
bash: Bourne Again Shell: the default shell on most Linux distributions and macOS.
zsh: Z shell: an extended Bourne shell with many improvements, popular as an interactive shell.
fish: Friendly Interactive Shell: a user-friendly shell with syntax highlighting and autosuggestions.
environment variable: A named value in a process's environment, used to configure programs at runtime.
path: The environment variable listing directories searched for executable commands.
alias: A shell shortcut that expands to a longer command.
pipe: A shell operator (|) that sends the output of one command as input to another.
redirect: A shell operator that sends command output to a file or device instead of the terminal.
glob: A pattern-matching syntax in shells using wildcards like * and ? to match filenames.
stdin: Standard input: the default input stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stdout: Standard output: the default output stream for a process, usually the terminal.
stderr: Standard error: the stream where a process writes error messages, separate from stdout.
exit code: A number returned by a process to indicate success (0) or failure (non-zero).
sudo: A program that allows a permitted user to execute a command as another user, typically root.
root: The superuser account on Unix-like systems with unrestricted access to the system.
user: A user account on a multi-user operating system, identified by a username and a numeric UID.
group: A collection of users in Unix-like systems, used to grant shared permissions.
permission: An access right on a file or directory, specifying read, write, and execute for user, group, and others.
umask: A value that determines the default permissions for newly created files and directories.
file system: The structure and rules an operating system uses to store and retrieve files on a storage device.
mount: The act of making a file system accessible at a directory in the operating system's tree.
partition: A logical division of a storage device that can hold a file system.
inode: A data structure on Unix-like file systems that stores metadata about a file (not its name).
symlink: A symbolic link: a special file that points to another file or directory.
hard link: A directory entry that points to the same inode as another file, effectively a second name for the same data.
tmpfs: A temporary file system stored in memory (RAM) rather than on persistent storage.
swap: Disk space used as virtual memory when physical RAM is exhausted.
daemon: A background process that runs without a controlling terminal, often providing a service.
process: A running instance of a program, with its own memory, file descriptors, and PID.
pid: Process ID: a numeric identifier assigned to each running process.
signal: A software interrupt delivered to a process to notify it of an event (e.g., SIGTERM, SIGKILL).
job: A process or pipeline managed by a shell's job control system.
cron: A time-based job scheduler on Unix-like systems that runs commands at specified intervals.
journalctl: A command-line tool to view logs collected by the systemd journal.
unit: A systemd configuration file describing a service, socket, device, mount, or other resource.
init: The first process started by the kernel on a Unix-like system, responsible for starting other processes.
init system: The software that initializes the system after the kernel boots and manages services.
bootloader: A program that loads the operating system kernel into memory at boot time.
grub: GRand Unified Bootloader: a widely used bootloader for Linux and other operating systems.
filesystem hierarchy: The standardized directory layout on Unix-like systems (e.g., /etc, /usr, /var).
pacman: The package manager for Arch Linux, used to install, update, and remove software.
aur: Arch User Repository: a community-driven repository of PKGBUILD files for Arch Linux.
pkgbuild: A shell script that describes how to build a package from source, used by makepkg.
makepkg: A script that automates building packages from PKGBUILDs on Arch Linux.
yay: Yet Another Yogurt: a popular AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Go.
paru: A feature-rich AUR helper for Arch Linux written in Rust.
reflector: A tool that retrieves and sorts Arch Linux mirror lists by speed and freshness.
base-devel: A package group on Arch Linux that provides essential tools for building packages from source.
arch wiki: The community-maintained documentation wiki for Arch Linux, widely used across Linux distributions.
apt: The package manager used on Debian and Ubuntu systems.
dpkg: The low-level package manager underlying apt on Debian-based systems.
yum: The legacy package manager for RPM-based distributions, superseded by dnf.
dnf: The modern package manager for Fedora and other RPM-based distributions.
rpm: RPM Package Manager: a package format and tool used by Fedora, RHEL, and SUSE.
snap: A universal package format developed by Canonical for Linux.
flatpak: A universal package format for Linux with sandboxing and per-app dependencies.
appimage: A portable Linux application format that runs without installation.
